newsitem.title: GREECE: Athens bourse mess unresolved, talks continue.
newsitem.headline: Athens bourse mess unresolved, talks continue.

text.p: The Athens bourse, rocked by one of the biggest upheavals in its history, appeared to opt for a compromise on Monday which would reverse billions of drachmas in trades over the past week.
The bourse has been closed for two working days because of an uproar following the failure of Delta Securities firm to pay 2.6 billion drachmas in settlements last week.
Delta's assets and accounts have been frozen, fraud charges laid and its senior officials ordered to stay in Greece.

After a daylong meeting on Monday, the Association of Athens Stock Exchange Members (SMEHA) appeared to endorse a plan for a group of 10 brokers that were the counter-parties in trades with Delta to effectively nullify recent trades and incur all losses.
Sources at the SMEHA meeting said the trade reversals would cover shares in textile firms Magrizos, Parnassos and Mills St. George from October 30 to November 6.

They said this would avoid turning to the exchange guarantee fund for a bailout -- a move which has been opposed vehemently by some SMEHA members -- and any losses would be covered by the firms involved.

SMEHA President Panagiotis Kondalexis told Reuters it was premature to name the brokerages involved in the trades with Delta. Sources at the SMEHA meeting said the names were cited and several Athens radio stations read out an unofficial list.
Kondalexis said he was discussing the matter with bourse President Manolis Xanthakis, who cut short a trip to Asia to fly home and oversee the crisis.
Sources at the SMEHA meeting told Reuters that the majority of the firms involved in trades with Delta had accepted the idea of reversing the trades and stomaching the losses themselves.
But, they said, a couple of state bank brokerages had to get clearance from higher ups.
Despite the upheavals, no official statements have been made during the day by the bourse, SMEHA or the national economy ministry -- which appoints the bourse president.
SMEHA also asked that a three-member committee of brokers oversee the exchange's clearing house which should settle its full backlog trades as soon as possible.
Clearing the backlog would also ensure that no payments were outstanding.
SMEHA also wanted auditors to audit all member firms on compliance with the clearing house and their clients, even if the bourse resumed trade.

Textile firm Magrizos, whose shares have been linked to the Delta default, said its shares' dramatic rise and fall over the past year may have been part of a "trading game" but denied any involvement.
"It could be that a trading game took place but we could neither intervene nor control it," David Magrizos, deputy managing director of Magrizos, told Reuters.

The Magrizos family owns more than 70 percent of the firm. Magrizos was trading at 201 drachmas a share in September 1995 and soared to a high of 1,365 in September 1996 before reversing course and closing at 911 drachmas on November 7.
"I believe the bourse should stay closed to facilitate cleansing, to end up with a better stock market," said Vassilis Hatzelias at Intersec Securities, a large brokerage.
He said SMEHA was opposed to tapping the exchange guarantee fund to bail out anyone caught in fraudulent trading practices.
Delta Securities, in the red with the clearing house for 2.6 billion drachmas, was charged with repeated fraud by the public prosecutor. --George Georgiopoulos, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
